newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Meridor denies economic plan in works.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Meridor denies economic plan in works.

text.p: Israeli Finance Minister Dan Meridor on Monday denied an Israeli newspaper report the government was working on a comprehensive programme to revitalise a sagging economy and boost exports.
The Maariv daily said the cabinet would meet this week to discuss a package of measures being put together by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, central bank Governor Jacob Frenkel and Meridor.

The paper said the measures include a widening of the bands in which the shekel can trade, liberalisation of foreign currency controls and a plan for capital market reform proposed last year by the Treasury but shelved by the government in November.
These measures would complement a cut in the 1997 budget and a reduction in interest rates, Maariv said.
When asked by reporters about the report Meridor replied: "I recommend you read Maariv because I don't know any of the details in this programme."
Meridor also said he did not believe any measures would be submitted to the cabinet this Friday as no meeting was scheduled for Friday.

The capital market reform had been shelved because a key recommendation -- taxing short-term savings-- was deemed too controversial. Maariv said Netanyahu would reopen discussion to overcome Meridor's opposition to widening the shekel's trading bands.
Speaking at a ceremony for the recent success of bank privatisations, Meridor said capital market reform continued to be an important goal of the Treasury.
"I intend to propose to the government what I already proposed and what is resting on its table since November. This has always been important."
He said a budget cut, if necessary, would be undertaken but had nothing to do with capital market reform.
"We are currently discussing details of an additional budget cut, its size and way of passing it through the cabinet," Meridor said.
This year's 197 billion shekel budget already includes reductions of seven billion shekels.

Meridor said the government had no intention of widening the shekel's bands. "The meaning of a widening of the bands is a worsening in the balance of payments situation and creating further difficulties in exports, creating the danger of a further economic slowdown and more unemployment," Meridor said.
"These are things we have already said, both I and the prime minister, and there's no change in this position."
